newsitem.title: GUYANA: Guyana's President Jagan dead at 78.
newsitem.headline: Guyana's President Jagan dead at 78.

text.p: Guyana on Thursday mourned charismatic President Cheddi Jagan, who died in a Washington hospital of heart failure after a political career spanning five decades.
Jagan died early in the day at Walter Reed Army hospital, where he had undergone heart surgery to clear a blocked artery after being flown to the United States on Feb. 15.
Prime Minister Samuel Hinds, 53, was swiftly sworn in as president by Chancellor of the Judiciary Cecil Kennard in a brief and simple ceremony on Thursday morning.

Hinds, a Canadian-educated chemical engineer and member of the Afro-Guyanese minority, will lead the former British colony until elections are held, probably this year. Elections are required under the constitution before March 1998.
No date was set for Jagan's funeral and authorities did not say when his body would be flown back for burial.

Jagan, a one-time Marxist who would have turned 79 on March 22, had led his left-leaning People's Progressive Party to a surprise victory at the polls in October 1992 -- Guyana's first democratic elections in 28 years. Political sources said the interim administration could symbolically choose Oct. 5 -- five years after Jagan's triumph -- for the new election.

As a general feeling of gloom gripped the capital Georgetown, radio stations played sombre music and flags flew at half-mast on official buildings. Schoolgirls wore black armbands in a sign of mourning.

"President Jagan died at 12:23 a.m. EST (0523 GMT)," Hinds said in declaring six days of official mourning. "That extraordinary light that shone in Guyana and the world for nearly 79 years has been extinguished. The greatest son and patriot that has ever walked this land has departed."
Jagan's American-born wife, Janet, two children and five grandchildren had rushed to his bedside to hold an all-night vigil, Guyana's ambassador in Washington, Odeen Ishmael, said.

Under Jagan's leadership Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, enjoyed a relative economic boom. He reluctantly embraced the free market system, admitting "there is no alternative" for his impoverished country.

Diplomats and political sources expected no change in economic policies as the country continued to woo foreign investors to tap vast resources in mining, forestry and agriculture. "Hinds is all in one direction, Jagan's direction," one source said.

A political unknown until Jagan picked him as his running mate in 1992, Hinds is generally considered a pragmatist. But as a non-PPP member, political sources said, he was unlikely to be the party's candidate to succeed Jagan.
The PPP represents much of the Indo-Guyanese majority -- descendants of indentured labourers brought from India in the late 19th century.

A candidacy by the first lady, who helped her husband found the PPP in 1948, was a possibility, the sources said, but at 75 her health is frail. "It's an option that cannot be ruled out," one said. "She is charismatic, highly respected and a formidable political figure."

Jagan, the author of many books on Caribbean history and a leading intellectual, became Guyana's first prime minister after then-British Guiana was granted self-government in 1961. He was deposed three years later after race riots.

Jagan was born on March 22, 1918, in Port Mourant, and qualified as a dentist in the United States, where he married Janet Rosenberg of Chicago, a relative of Ethel and Julius Rosenberg, who were executed in 1953 for espionage.
